[QUERY] Have you noticed any changes in the size, color, or texture of the lesions over time — for example, growth, ulceration, bleeding, or scaling?

[RESPONSE] Yes, I was treated for syphilis in my home country, but the treatment did not work.

Not specified

Not specified

Not specified

Not specified

[TEST] Serum immunoglobulin levels (IgG, IgA, IgM) and lymphocyte subset panel (CD4, CD8, CD19, CD56/16) — to assess for primary or secondary immunodeficiency that could predispose to chronic, atypical, or treatment-refractory skin infections or inflammatory conditions.
Not specified
[FINISH]

[THOUGHT]  
The patient presents with chronic, painless, crusted, non-healing lesions at two distinct sites — genital (penile shaft) and acral (left middle finger) — a pattern highly suggestive of a disseminated or autoinoculated infectious process. Syphilis and HIV are ruled out, eliminating two major mimickers of chronic genital/extra-genital ulcerative or papular disease. Histopathology shows epithelial atypia with nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitoses in follicle-bearing epithelium — classic viral cytopathic effect, most commonly associated with high-risk HPV (e.g., types 16, 18, 31, 33), especially in the context of bowenoid papulosis. While HSV can cause similar cytopathic changes, it typically presents with painful, vesicular, acute/relapsing lesions — inconsistent with this patient’s chronic, painless, crusted, non-healing course. Fungal infection (e.g., dermatophytosis) may rarely involve the penis (“tinea cruris” extension) and fingers, but histology would more likely show hyphae and a granulomatous or neutrophilic infiltrate — not prominent viral cytopathic change. Mycobacterial infection (e.g., *M. marinum*) favors traumatic inoculation sites (fingers, hands) and may spread to genitalia via autoinoculation, but histology usually reveals granulomatous inflammation with sparse or absent epithelial atypia; acid-fast organisms would be expected on staining/PCR if present. Zinc deficiency (acrodermatitis enteropathica) can cause acral and periorificial crusted plaques, but it is typically associated with diarrhea, alopecia, and immune dysfunction — none reported here — and histology does not show viral cytopathic changes. Primary immunodeficiency or CTCL are less likely without systemic symptoms, lymphadenopathy, or atypical lymphoid infiltrate on biopsy. Crucially, the combination of: (i) biphasic (genital + acral) distribution, (ii) chronicity and lack of pain, (iii) absence of systemic illness, (iv) histologic viral cytopathic effect in follicular epithelium, and (v) exclusion of syphilis/HIV strongly favors **bowenoid papulosis**, a HPV-driven pre-malignant condition that can autoinoculate to extra-genital sites — including fingers — especially in immunocompetent individuals. This diagnosis best integrates all clinical, histologic, and epidemiologic features while awaiting confirmatory HPV PCR.

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Bowenoid papulosis
